title: Start Here: Why Scams Work
summary: The scammer's playbook, and your permission to hang up.

responses.situation: Your phone rings. A calm, official-sounding man says: "This is the fraud department at your bank. Your account is being drained right now. Don't hang up, or you could lose everything."

options.text: "Oh no! What do I need to do?"
options.feedback: This is exactly what he wants. Now he's in charge of the conversation, and the next step will be a code, a "safe account," or gift cards.

options.text: "How do I know you're really from my bank?"
options.feedback: A fair question, but it keeps you on the line, and scammers always have a convincing answer ready. You don't need to win an argument. You just need to hang up.

options.text: "I'm going to hang up and call the number on the back of my card." (Then hang up.)
options.feedback: Perfect. If there's a real problem, your bank will still be there when you call. A real bank will never be upset that you checked.

responses.situation: A crying voice that sounds like your grandson says: "Grandma, I'm in trouble and I need money for bail. Please don't tell Mom and Dad. I'm so embarrassed."

options.text: "Oh honey, of course. How much do you need?"
options.feedback: Love makes us want to help right away. That's the feeling scammers are counting on. Voices can now be copied with AI, so even a familiar voice needs checking.

options.text: "I love you. I'm going to hang up and call you right back on your own phone." (Then call him, or his parents.)
options.feedback: Exactly right. A real grandchild will understand. If the call was a scam, you'll find out in one quick phone call. Better still, ask for your family code word.

options.text: "I won't tell anyone. Where should I send it?"
options.feedback: "Keep it a secret" is one of the biggest warning signs there is. Scammers want to keep you away from the people who would spot the scam.

responses.situation: A friendly caller offers you a free medical alert system "covered by Medicare." When you hesitate, she says, "It will only take a minute. I just need your Medicare number. You wouldn't want to miss out, would you?"

options.text: "No, thank you." (Then hang up, without waiting for her to finish.)
options.feedback: That's all it takes. You don't owe a stranger a reason, and hanging up isn't rude. It's smart.

options.text: "I'm sorry, I don't think so. Could you tell me a little more first?"
options.feedback: Apologizing and asking for more information keeps the door open. A pushy caller will use every extra minute to wear you down.

options.text: "I don't want to be rude... I suppose I can give you the number."
options.feedback: Being polite to a scammer only helps the scammer. Your Medicare number is like a credit card number. Never give it to someone who called you.

responses.situation: Someone you've been chatting with online for two months says they love you. Now they need $3,000 for a medical bill and say, "If you really cared about me, you'd help."

options.text: Send a smaller amount so they don't feel hurt.
options.feedback: Any amount leads to another request, and then another. Guilt ("if you really cared") is a pressure tactic, not love.

options.text: "I don't send money to anyone I haven't met in person. I'm going to talk this over with my daughter."
options.feedback: A clear, kind boundary. Someone who truly cares about you will respect it. A scammer will get angry, push harder, or disappear.

options.text: Ask them to promise they'll pay it back.
options.feedback: Promises cost a scammer nothing. The money would be gone the moment you sent it.

lesson.intro: Scams don't work because people are foolish. They work because scammers are professionals who use the same playbook again and again, and because most of us were raised to be polite, helpful, and trusting. Those are good qualities. Scammers count on them.

sections.heading: The scammer's playbook
paragraphs: Almost every scam uses some of these tricks. Once you know them, you'll start to see them everywhere.
bullets: Stir up strong feelings: fear, panic, excitement, or love. When we're upset or excited, it's much harder to think clearly. Research shows scammers deliberately use this.
Rush you: "right now," "within the hour," "before it's too late."
Pretend to be someone in charge: your bank, the police, the government, Microsoft.
Ask for secrecy: "Don't tell your family," "don't tell the bank teller."
Use your good manners: they know polite people don't like to interrupt, hang up, or say no.

sections.heading: Why it's so hard to hang up
paragraphs: Many of us were taught it's rude to hang up on someone, to interrupt, or to say no without a good reason. Scammers know this. They keep talking, ask friendly questions, act hurt, or get angry, all to keep you on the line.
Here's the truth: being polite to a scammer only helps the scammer. The longer the call, the more chances they have to wear you down.

sections.heading: Your permission slip
bullets: You may hang up without saying goodbye.
You don't owe a stranger an explanation. "No, thank you" is a complete answer.
It's always okay to say "I need to talk to my family first." A real company will wait.
Real banks, agencies, and family members will never be upset that you hung up and called them back to check.
Letting unknown numbers go to voicemail is perfectly fine. Real callers leave a message.

sections.heading: The rule to remember: Pause, Hang up, Check
paragraphs: Whenever you feel rushed, scared, excited, or told to keep a secret: pause. Hang up, or don't reply. Then check, by calling a number you already know or by talking to someone you trust.
And if you were ever fooled, it's not your fault. Scams fool doctors, lawyers, and police officers too. Report it and tell someone. That's how scams are stopped.

lesson.keyPoint: Strong feelings + hurry + secrecy = scam. You always have permission to hang up and check.

actions: Keep a short "no" script by the phone (see the phrases below)
Let unknown numbers go to voicemail. Real callers leave a message
Hang up the moment you feel rushed, scared, or told to keep a secret
Call back using a number you already know, never one the caller gives you
Before sending money or sharing information, talk it over with someone you trust
If you were tricked, it's not your fault. Report it and tell someone
sayThis: No, thank you. (Then hang up.)
I don't do business over the phone. I'll call the number on my statement.
I never make decisions on the phone. I talk to my family first.
Please take me off your list. I'm hanging up now.

title: Phishing Emails
summary: Fake emails that pretend to be your bank, Amazon, or another company you trust.

lesson.intro: Phishing (say it like "fishing") is when a scammer sends an email that looks like it's from a company you trust. They want you to click a link, open an attachment, or type in a password or card number.

sections.heading: What phishing emails look like
paragraphs: Scammers copy real logos and colors, so an email can look exactly like one from your bank or Amazon. The trick is in the details.
bullets: The sender's address is a little off, like "amaz0n-ship.com" (a zero instead of an "o") or a free Gmail or Outlook address
It creates a panic: "Your account will be locked in 24 hours" or "You were charged $849"
It starts with "Dear Customer" instead of your name
It asks you to click a link to "verify," "confirm," or "cancel"

sections.heading: Why it works
paragraphs: Scammers count on you acting fast before you stop to think. A fake charge or a locked account makes anyone want to fix it right away. That rush is exactly what they want.

sections.heading: The safe habit
paragraphs: Never use the links, phone numbers, or attachments in a surprise email. Instead, go to the company yourself: type the website address you already know, open their app, or call the number on the back of your card or on a past statement.

lesson.keyPoint: If an email rushes you to click, stop. Go to the company yourself instead of using the email.

actions: Don't click links or open attachments in the email
Check the sender's full email address, not just the name
Contact the company using a phone number or website you already trust
If you clicked or typed a password, change that password right away
If you shared a card or bank number, call your bank using the number on your card
Forward phishing emails to reportphishing@apwg.org, then delete them
sayThis: (To yourself) "I'll go to the company's website myself instead of clicking."
(To family) "Can you look at this email with me before I do anything?"

title: Text Message Scams
summary: Fake texts about packages, tolls, bank alerts, and "wrong numbers."

lesson.intro: Text message scams (sometimes called "smishing") work just like phishing emails, but they arrive on your phone. Because texts feel personal and urgent, they can be even more convincing.

sections.heading: Common scam texts
bullets: "Your package can't be delivered. Pay a $1.99 fee here."
"You owe an unpaid toll. Pay now to avoid a penalty."
"Did you make a $500 purchase? Reply YES or NO." (pretending to be your bank)
A friendly "wrong number" text that turns into a long chat, then a money or investment pitch

sections.heading: What gives them away
paragraphs: Real companies rarely text you a link to pay a fee. The link usually goes to a strange web address, not the company's real site. Even replying "STOP" or "NO" tells the scammer your number is active.

sections.heading: The safe habit
paragraphs: Don't tap links in surprise texts and don't reply. If you're worried about a package, toll, or bank charge, check by going to the company's real website or app, or by calling a number you trust.

lesson.keyPoint: Don't tap, don't reply. Check with the company yourself, using a number or app you trust.

actions: Don't tap any links in the text
Don't reply, not even "STOP" or "wrong number"
Forward the text to 7726 (it spells SPAM) to report it to your phone company
Delete the text and block the number
Check any package, toll, or bank issue using the company's real app or website
If you entered card details, call your bank right away
sayThis: Say nothing at all. You never owe a stranger a reply, not even "wrong number."
(To family) "I got a strange text. Does this look real to you?"

title: Phone & Voice Scams
summary: Calls from "family in trouble," fake bank fraud departments, and AI voice copies.

lesson.intro: Some of the most costly scams start with a phone call. A calm, confident voice, or a frightened one that sounds like a family member, can be very hard to say no to.

sections.heading: The "grandparent" scam and AI voice copies
paragraphs: A caller says they're your grandchild (or a lawyer or police officer for them). There's been an accident or an arrest, they need money right now, and they beg you not to tell anyone.
Today, scammers can copy a real person's voice using a few seconds of video from social media. The voice may truly sound like someone you love.

sections.heading: Fake bank and "fraud department" calls
paragraphs: A caller says they're from your bank's fraud team. They say your account is under attack and you must move your money to a "safe account," or read them a code that was just texted to you. A real bank will never ask you to do either.

sections.heading: Caller ID can lie
paragraphs: Scammers can make any name or number appear on your screen, even your bank's real number or "Police." Don't trust caller ID on its own.

sections.heading: The safe habit
paragraphs: Hang up and call back using a number you already know. Call your grandchild or their parents directly. Agree on a family code word ahead of time that a real family member would know.
bullets: Nobody legitimate asks to be paid with gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency, or cash picked up by a courier
Never read a texted verification code to someone who called you

lesson.keyPoint: Hang up and call back on a number you know. Secrecy and rush are signs of a scam.

actions: Hang up. You don't need to be polite to a scammer
Call the person or company back using a number you already have
Ask a question only the real person would know, or use your family code word
Never pay with gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency, or cash by courier
Never share a code that was texted to you
Add your number to the Do Not Call Registry at donotcall.gov or 1-888-382-1222
sayThis: "I don't do business over the phone. I'll call you back at the number on my card."
"What's our family code word?"
"I'm hanging up now."

title: Tech-Support Pop-ups
summary: Scary warnings on your screen that tell you to call "Microsoft" or "Apple."

lesson.intro: A tech-support scam starts with a loud, scary warning that suddenly fills your screen. It says your computer is infected and you must call a phone number right away.

sections.heading: What the warning looks like
bullets: Red warning signs, flashing text, or a beeping or talking alarm
Microsoft, Apple, or Windows logos to look official
A phone number to call "Certified Technicians"
"Do not turn off your computer" or "Do not close this window"

sections.heading: What really happens if you call
paragraphs: The "technician" asks you to install a program so they can control your computer. They show you fake problems, charge you for repairs you don't need, and may get into your bank accounts. Some then call back later pretending to offer a refund.

sections.heading: The truth
paragraphs: Microsoft and Apple never put phone numbers in error messages, and they never call you out of the blue. The warning is just a web page. Your computer is almost always fine.

lesson.keyPoint: Never call a number from a pop-up. Close the browser, and your computer is almost always fine.

actions: Don't call the number and don't click anything on the warning
Close the web browser. If it won't close, restart the computer
Never let a stranger connect to your computer remotely
If you already let someone in, turn off the computer and have a trusted person check it
Change your passwords from a different device, and call your bank if you paid anything
Keep your computer's automatic updates turned on
sayThis: (To a "technician") "No. I don't let anyone into my computer."
"I'm hanging up and calling my family."

title: Government Impostor Scams
summary: Fake calls and letters from the IRS, Social Security, and Medicare.

lesson.intro: Scammers love to pretend to be the government, because people take official warnings seriously. They threaten arrest, lost benefits, or legal trouble unless you act right now.

sections.heading: What the real agencies will NOT do
bullets: The IRS will not call to demand immediate payment, threaten arrest, or ask for gift cards, wire transfers, or cryptocurrency
Social Security will not "suspend" your Social Security number or threaten you
Medicare will not call you out of the blue to ask for your Medicare number
No government agency will ask you to pay at a Bitcoin ATM or keep the call secret

sections.heading: How they really reach you
paragraphs: If the IRS needs to reach you about taxes you owe, it usually starts by sending a letter in the mail. Real agencies give you time, explain your rights, and let you call them back.

sections.heading: The safe habit
paragraphs: Hang up, and call the agency yourself using the official number below. If the problem is real, they will tell you.
bullets: Social Security: 1-800-772-1213
Medicare: 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227)

lesson.keyPoint: Government agencies don't threaten, rush, or ask for gift cards. Hang up and call the official number.

actions: Hang up or don't reply
Don't give your Social Security, Medicare, or bank numbers to anyone who contacted you
Call the agency yourself using the official number on its .gov website
Report IRS impostors at tigta.gov and Social Security impostors at oig.ssa.gov
Report it to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov
If you paid with a gift card, call the card company right away and keep the receipt
sayThis: "I'll call the agency myself at the official number."
"I don't pay anything over the phone. Send me a letter."

title: Online Marketplace Scams
summary: Tricks on Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, and online shopping sites.

lesson.intro: Buying and selling online is handy, and scammers know it. Whether you're the buyer or the seller, a few tricks show up again and again.

sections.heading: When you're selling
bullets: A "buyer" sends a check for MORE than your price and asks you to send back the difference. The check later bounces, and you lose the money
A "buyer" asks you to read them a code sent to your phone "to prove you're real." That code lets them take over your account

sections.heading: When you're buying
bullets: Prices that are far too good to be true, like a puppy, car, or concert tickets for a fraction of the normal cost
The seller can't meet in person and wants a deposit first
They push you to pay with Zelle, Venmo, gift cards, or a wire transfer, which are hard to get back

sections.heading: The safe habit
paragraphs: Meet in a public place (many police stations have safe exchange spots), see the item before you pay, and pay in person. When buying from a website, use a credit card, which gives you the most protection.

lesson.keyPoint: See it before you pay, never accept overpayments, and never share a code texted to you.

actions: Don't send money back from an overpayment, and don't ship before the payment truly clears
Never share a verification code texted to your phone
Meet in a public place and see the item before you pay
Use a credit card for online purchases
Report the account to the marketplace and block it
If you paid, contact your bank or payment app right away
sayThis: "I only do cash or in-app payment, in person."
"I never share codes from my phone."

title: Romance Scams
summary: Online "sweethearts" who build trust and then ask for money.

lesson.intro: Romance scammers create fake online profiles to build a loving relationship. It can last weeks or months. Then there's an emergency, and they need money. These scams cause some of the biggest losses, and the heartbreak too.

sections.heading: Warning signs
bullets: They say "I love you" very quickly
They live far away: overseas, on an oil rig, or in the military
They always have a reason they can't video chat or meet in person
They ask you to move from the dating site to texting or WhatsApp
There's suddenly an emergency: medical bills, customs fees, a plane ticket to finally visit
They offer to teach you about investing in cryptocurrency

sections.heading: Why kind people fall for it
paragraphs: These scammers are professionals who use scripts. They're patient and attentive, and they make you feel special. Being fooled has nothing to do with being foolish.

sections.heading: The safe habit
paragraphs: Never send money, gift cards, or crypto to someone you have only met online. Talk to a trusted friend or family member about a new online relationship. Scammers will try to keep it secret.

lesson.keyPoint: Never send money to someone you've only met online, no matter how real the relationship feels.

actions: Stop sending money and stop sharing personal information
Talk to a trusted friend or family member about it
Do a reverse image search on their photos (a family member can help)
Report the profile to the dating site or social media app
Report it to the FBI at ic3.gov and the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov
If you sent money, call your bank or the payment company right away
sayThis: "I don't send money to anyone I haven't met in person."
"Let's video chat first."
"I talk about big decisions with my family."

title: Investment & Crypto Scams
summary: "Guaranteed" returns, crypto ATMs, and fake trading apps.

lesson.intro: Investment scams promise to grow your money quickly and safely. Today many use cryptocurrency, because it's hard to trace and nearly impossible to get back.

sections.heading: Warning signs
bullets: "Guaranteed" returns, "no risk," or doubling your money
Pressure to invest right now before you "miss out"
A new online friend or "mentor" who wants to teach you to trade
A trading website or app that shows big gains, but you have to pay "fees" or "taxes" to withdraw
Being told to pay at a Bitcoin ATM or to move your savings into crypto

sections.heading: The "recovery" trap
paragraphs: After a loss, scammers may contact you again pretending to be lawyers or agents who can get your money back for an upfront fee. That's a second scam.

sections.heading: The safe habit
paragraphs: Check anyone offering investments at brokercheck.finra.org and investor.gov. Talk to someone you trust before moving any savings. Real investments never come with guarantees.

lesson.keyPoint: Guaranteed returns and crypto pressure mean scam. Check first, and never pay to withdraw your own money.

actions: Don't send more money, even if the app says you need to pay a fee to withdraw
Never use a Bitcoin ATM because someone told you to
Look up the person or company at brokercheck.finra.org and investor.gov
Talk to a trusted family member or your own financial advisor
Report it at ic3.gov and reportfraud.ftc.gov
Beware of anyone who offers to recover your lost money for a fee
sayThis: "I never invest over the phone or through an app someone sends me."
"I'll check with my own advisor first."
"I don't use Bitcoin ATMs."
